Q2336216.summary: At the centre of this great embroidered hanging, a youthful, beardless Christ holds an open book within a medallion, surrounded by wedge-shaped scenes of the days of Creation. A Latin inscription from the opening of Genesis runs around the circle, and in the border appear the winds and the months of the year, figures of the ordered cosmos. The whole work presents Christ as the creating Word through whom all things were made.
facts: Despite its name, the work is couched needlework laid on a woollen ground rather than a woven tapestry; it measures 3.65 × 4.70 m.
The right-hand border and the lower third are lost; scholars believe the missing part may have shown the finding of the True Cross and the remaining months.
It was restored in 1880 and again in the early 20th century, in 1952 and in 1975.
Q2336216.notes: Wikipedia dates it to the 11th century in its lead but says it is widely agreed to be late 11th or early 12th century. A detail photograph of the central Christ is also in the collection as commons:126502123 (undated); that entry duplicates this work.

cur:legends-madonna-di-san-luca.summary: Encased in a silver revetment with crowns, pearls and votive jewels, only the painted faces of the Virgin and the Christ Child look out from Bologna's most beloved icon, a Hodegetria in which Mary holds the blessing Child. A fifteenth-century legend tells that a Greek pilgrim brought it from Hagia Sophia in Constantinople as a work of St Luke, with instructions to place it on the 'mount of the Guard'. Study of the panel suggests that the visible painting is by a Western hand of around 1200, painted over an older Byzantine-style image, and it has been carried in procession to the city every year since 1433.
facts: X-ray studies revealed an earlier painting beneath the visible one, Byzantine in style and close to surviving copies of the icon of the Virgin in Hagia Sophia; the use of indigo for the Virgin's robe supports an eastern origin for that first layer.
The annual procession began after the 'miracle of the rain' of 5 July 1433, when spring rains threatening the harvest stopped as the icon entered the city.

The sanctuary on the Colle della Guardia is reached by a covered portico about 3.8 km long, begun in 1674 to shelter pilgrims and the icon's annual procession; it was inscribed in 2021 among the UNESCO World Heritage Porticoes of Bologna.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-148-chris.summary: The focus of the drawing is the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, seated in a globe-mandorla supported by angels, with a band of stars below and great personifications holding the sun and moon at either end of the sky. Beneath him the whole creation praises him as the psalm commands: mountains and hills with fruitful trees and cedars, beasts, creeping things and birds, and groups of kings, soldiers, young men and maidens, old men and children. A close parallel appears in the Stuttgart Psalter.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-148-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-faras-christ-enthroned.summary: This tall panel of detached wall painting, over three metres high, preserves parts of a large composition that the museum identifies as Christ enthroned with angels, the cross and apostles: the richly patterned, striped robes of a monumental figure fill the upper part, with a cross and smaller figures below. Though much of the paint surface is lost, its scale conveys the grandeur of the decoration of the cathedral of Pachoras.
facts: Faras (ancient Pachoras), a major city of Christian Nubia, was flooded by Lake Nasser in the 1960s; before that, a Polish team led by Kazimierz Michałowski excavated its cathedral (1960–64) during UNESCO's Nubian salvage campaign, and the paintings were divided between Khartoum and Warsaw.
The museum catalogue describes the subject as 'Christ Enthroned, Angels, the Cross, Apostles' and gives its height as 316 cm.

Q1527541.summary: In the darkness of the stable the only true light comes from the newborn Christ, glowing so brightly that Mary's face is illuminated and a woman beside the shepherds shields her eyes. Above, a swirl of angels tumbles through the night sky while dawn breaks faintly over the hills. Correggio's luminous nocturne made the Child himself the source of light — the Light of the World — and was endlessly admired by later painters.
facts: It was commissioned in October 1522 by Alberto Pratoneri for his family chapel in the church of San Prospero in Reggio Emilia, and was installed there in 1530.

In 1640 Duke Francesco I d'Este took the painting from its church for his gallery in Modena; in 1745–46 it was among the hundred masterpieces of the Este collection sold to Augustus III, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland.
It is one of the most celebrated night scenes of Renaissance painting, and anticipates the dramatic lighting of the Baroque.

Q2472983.summary: Tintoretto sets the table on a steep diagonal in a dim, crowded room, where Christ, haloed in light, gives bread to his disciples while servants bustle about. Light and smoke from a hanging lamp seem to dissolve into a host of translucent angels. In contrast to Leonardo's focus on the betrayal, this is a mystical vision of the institution of the Eucharist.
facts: It was one of Tintoretto's last works, completed in the year of his death, 1594.
It was painted for the presbytery of Andrea Palladio's church of San Giorgio Maggiore, where it still hangs.
The diagonal composition draws the viewer into the scene, a dramatic departure from the frontal Last Suppers of the High Renaissance.
